paragraphs.text: Lovers of Christ, I have marvelled with you at the new things of the grace of the Gospel, proclaimed through the Old Testament. My mind has been enlightened with yours as I saw the stamp of the apostles shining out in the voices of the prophets. I confess the gain, so that I may receive the reward. I saw strange mysteries proclaimed through the Old Testament: Abraham swearing by the thigh, putting forward the thigh, yet calling on the Maker of heaven and earth as witness to his word. For he says, “Put your hand under my thigh, and swear to me by God, who made heaven and earth.” But a question arises. If this was said on account of the seed that was to blossom from the thighs of Jacob, as in the words, “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs,” how then will the oath be found to be by the Savior? For Isaac had already been born and the seed had already come forth, and when the oath was made there was no longer any hope of seed in Abraham’s thigh. Yet Abraham had within himself the saving seed, of which Paul says, “It was spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” And weighing the letter and interpreting it, he says in the Letter to the Galatians: “It does not say, ‘And to your seeds,’ as of many, but ‘And to your seed,’ who is Christ.” It has therefore been shown that Christ is the seed of Abraham according to the flesh, and so the oath was fittingly made by the seed. But the question remains: how could he swear by the thigh, when the saving flower had already come forth? It is because that member had once become an instrument, and the divine seed had once dwelt there, so he swears by it as by a temple. And whoever swears by the temple swears by the one who has dwelt in it. Who bears witness to this statement? Our Savior himself, when he says to the Pharisees: “Woe to you, foolish and blind Pharisees, for you say, ‘If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing; but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound.’” And what does he say next? “Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gold, or the temple that made the gold holy? Therefore I tell you: whoever swears by the temple swears by the one who has dwelt in it.”

A royal house, once it has received a king, is set apart once for all because it has at some time received a king, even if the king leaves the dwelling a second or a third time. In the same way the members of the patriarch, by having once become instruments of the dispensation that was to come, were a temple of the promised benefit. And the oath is not unjust; it is true testimony. So he makes him swear by the seed, and he explains what the seed is: "Put your hand under my thigh," he says, "and I will make you swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and of earth." Our Saviour, then, is God of heaven and earth. This is also why, in Zechariah the prophet, when various visions were sent and appeared to the holy man, this was one part of a vision: "And I lifted up my eyes," he says, "and saw, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, with seven lamps on top of the lampstand, seven oil-funnels for the lamps, and seven torches, and on the right of the lampstand and on its left two olive branches. And I said to the angel who was speaking with me, 'Lord, what are these?'" It was a vision that showed some things and pointed to others for their interpretation, and the things that appeared did not signify themselves but pointed to something else. So the prophet asks, "Lord, what are these?" If he had been asking about what appeared, his question would have been a poor one. Do you not know what a lampstand is, or an olive tree? No, the prophet is seeking not what appears but what is to be contemplated: "What are these?" And the angel says, "Do you not know what these are?" "No, lord." He frankly admits his ignorance and is taught by the truth. He too is a brother of the eunuch who heard from Philip, "Do you understand what you are reading?" and frankly replied, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" "Do you not know what these are?" And he says, "No, lord." "Who are the two olive branches on the right and on the left of the lampstand?" "These are the two sons of fatness, who stand beside the Lord of the whole earth." In explaining the olive trees he also explains, along with them, what the lampstand is.

Pay close attention. The lampstand stood there, and the branches stood beside the lampstand. Yet when the angel explains them, he does not show the olive trees standing beside a lampstand but beside God. So the lampstand is a type of God, or rather of our Saviour and of his dispensation in the flesh. "Do you not know what these are?" "No, lord." "These branches are the two sons of fatness, who stand beside the Lord of the whole earth": not beside the lampstand, as it appeared, but beside "the Lord of the whole earth." He presents a lampstand with seven lights because of the Lord's dispensation in the flesh. For the Lord's flesh was a true lampstand, which displayed the illuminations of the Holy Spirit in sevenfold grace. "A rod shall come forth," says Isaiah, "from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from it, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him." Which Spirit? The one that is manifold in its operations and simple in its nature. "The Spirit of God shall rest upon him": here he expresses the essence, the Holy Spirit himself. What follows speaks of the Spirit's operations: "the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, the spirit of the fear of God." The seven graces of the Holy Spirit, the seven operations that rested upon the Lord's body, are what he portrays in the figure of the lamps. And why seven lamps? Because the operation of the Holy Spirit gives light. Then, a little further on, he says again: "These are the seven eyes of the Lord, which look upon the whole earth."

Do you see how the truth makes itself clear by itself and has no need of human reasonings? "But they stand beside the Lord of the whole earth." Zechariah calls the Saviour Lord of the whole earth with reference to his dispensation in the flesh. Peter, the chief of the apostles, speaking with Cornelius, says: "We know the thing that took place throughout Judea, Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit." And again the same apostle says: "the thing that took place throughout all Judea," and "the word that God sent, proclaiming the good news of peace to the children of Israel: he is Lord of all." The prophet says "Lord of the earth," and Peter the evangelist calls him "Lord of all." "He is Lord of all": of all things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, things visible and invisible. He is Lord of all. This is why John speaks in harmony with this when he says, "He who comes from above is above all."

We must now examine this carefully and put an end to the heretics' wrangling. They follow the apostle's words wrongly, and instead of understanding them piously they distort them impiously. So the children of the heretics think that he received being raised above all as a reward for the cross, and that God highly exalted him because he suffered and endured the cross. They follow the apostle's words without grasping their meaning; they have followed the letter without testing the sense. The passage runs as follows: "He humbled himself to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him." No doubt, heretic, you say this was because of the passion, as if God gave him exaltation as a reward for his suffering. "And he gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth." "Do you see," he says, "that he was exalted after the cross? Do you see that after the passion he received exaltation as his reward?" Well, if he was exalted after the cross, as you claim, why did John the Baptist say before the passion, before the cross, "He who comes from above is above all"? He said "is," not "becomes." This is also why Jesus, speaking with the Jews, said, "Truly, truly I tell you, before Abraham came to be, I am." For he always is, and was, and will be, and will have no end. But, brothers, we must pay our debt, and not use our digressions as a pretext for going back on our promises. Let the glory of Christ and the majesty of the Father be proclaimed. Let the Holy Spirit be proclaimed, let the Only-begotten be exalted, let the Father be glorified. Let no one think the order of dignity has been overturned if we mention the Spirit first, then the Son, then the Father, or the Son first, or the Father. For the divine nature has no order: not because it is disorderly, but because it transcends order. God is not a shape, not because he is unseemly but because he is without shape; God has no form, not because he is formless but because he is incorporeal. In the same way the divine nature has no order, not because it is disorderly but because it transcends order.

I name the Father first, not first in order but first in thought, since he is the begetter of the Only-begotten, the root of the holy fruit, eternal light that begot eternal light. My brothers, suppose one of us tried today, in church, among an orthodox people, a people filled with all right knowledge, to place the Son before the Father: would he not be accused of blasphemy by the orthodox themselves? If someone dared to say in church, "May Christ and his Father bless you," would he not be thought disorderly for failing to put the root first and only then add the fruit? If someone said, "The Son and the Father will save us," would he not be thought to be causing confusion and violating the order? That is what thoughtless judges would think. But in the judgment of truth, which wins the victory by the apostle's vote, it makes no difference whether one mentions the Son first, or the Father, or the Spirit. Listen to how Paul, the great herald, puts it when writing to the Thessalonians: "Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father sanctify us." The Son first and the Father second. (O soul filled with a holy lamp!) For there is no order in the holy nature. Whatever is placed first is understood as equal in honour, the second is not diminished, and the third is not insulted. So he uses the names without distinction, because he knows that the nature is undivided and the kingdom indivisible. Let us ask the holy Paul where he got the grounds for speaking of God in this way, or giving glory in this way, or placing the Son before the Father, not in order or in power but in wording. Why did he mention the Son first and then the Father? Let Paul answer in his own defence and teach the Church: "I say nothing of my own; Christ dictates these doctrines through me. Or do you want proof that Christ is speaking in me? Christ speaks through me. Do not accuse me; do not find fault with the Master's voice. But can you not understand that Christ speaks through me? Then listen to him speaking plainly in his own person." If the names of the Holy Trinity were subject to order, so that the one named first was first in power, the second second in rank, and the third third by being lesser, would not the Saviour himself, who is the Truth, have been confusing the word of truth? And where did the Saviour mention himself first and then the Father? "If anyone keeps my commandments," he says, "I and the Father will come and make our home with him."

"But he overstepped the order," say the children of the heretics, who would have the Son be something like a king's prefect in relation to the Father. Let them be asked whether a prefect ever dared to say of the king, "I and the king issue this decree." Understand what is above us from what is among us. Would a created nature put itself before the uncreated? Would a created nature, as you call it, have dared to count itself alongside that incomparable supremacy and say, "We will come and make our home with him"? No: by "I and the Father" he showed that the order of the names makes no difference, and by "We will come and make our home" he showed that their activity is equal in honour. So too in another passage, when the apostle Philip says, "Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us," the Saviour answers, "Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you do not know me?" The answer seems contrary to the question. "Surely I did not ask about you? I said, 'Show us the Father.'" Yet he says, "Have I been with you all this time, and you do not know me?" If he is unlike the Father, how is the unlike shown through the unlike? How is the great one seen through the small one? How is the one superior in dignity seen through the one who is diminished, or the Creator through the servant? "I have been with you all this time." He did not say, "The Father is with you," but "I am." For where I am, the Father is. "Have I been with you all this time, and you do not know me?" "You do not know me" is well said. Philip says "Show," and the Saviour says "You do not know me?", because he wants to show that God is made present not by sight but by knowledge. "Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?" Again "I" comes first, and then "the Father." "I am in the Father and the Father is in me. How then can you say, 'Show us the Father'?" That is, "How could you expect to see him as someone other?" "I am in the Father and the Father is in me": the Son is known through the Father and the Father through the Son. "How can you say 'Show us,' as though you were seeking to see the Father as someone other than me? I am in the Father and the Father is in me." This does not mean that the nature is mixed together, or that it is like one bowl set inside another. "I am in the Father and the Father is in me." He is not speaking of bodies joined together; this is a matter of contemplating ideas.

"I am in the Father," for the Father is not known without the Son; "and the Father is in me," for the Son does not appear without the Father, just as the mind is seen in the word and the word in the mind. How can I know what you are thinking, except through what you say? Your word presents your mind, and your mind in turn interprets your word. One cannot see a word without grasping the thought, nor grasp the thought unless the word has expressed it. This is why the evangelist says, "In the beginning was the Word": to show that the begetting involved no passion. What a word is to the mind, the only-begotten Word is to the Father. And here is the wonder (I will go back over some of what was said earlier). It was said before that from what is among us you will learn how things above us are. While the word is within, with the mind that begets it, is it a visible thing with a visible thing? No, it is invisible with the invisible, intelligible with the intelligible, incorporeal with the incorporeal. But when the word is about to go forth, it passes to the mouth and there clothes itself with voice. No other nature supplies it with the voice; the word itself weaves its own speech. So too he who is invisible in his nature with the Father put on the voice and came forth, and he who was previously unseen became plain to all. Then, having come forth, he fills all things, yet does not leave the mind that begot him.

For what human being, when he speaks a word and teaches others, empties himself of that word? If I say something and it reaches the ears of others, has it left my mind empty? Has the word not gone forth outside and yet remained within? Has it not filled countless ears without departing from the one who begot it? So a human word, sent out by the one who begets it, both goes forth outside and does not abandon its begetter. And did God the Word, when he appeared in the world for our sake, leave the Father's bosom empty? Not at all. And here is the wonder: tens of thousands hear the one Word of God, and though he reaches so many he is not divided. He is wholly with each of us who hear him, and wholly with all. Did the Father then beget by flowing out and cutting off, and was he divided and split apart, as they say? Let the Saviour say to them, "Search the Scriptures." Search them; do not corrupt them. Search them, not merely reading them but tracking down the depths of their meaning. God gave the Scriptures, but he did not lay bare their deeper sense. He left that for you to pursue, in order to test your good sense and see your diligence, to see whether you serve the Scriptures or do violence to them. Just as God set before us the nature of things but hid the arts, so that everything was brought forth by God while art was born of human thought, so it is with the Scriptures.

Let me make this clear. God gave stones; God gave the nature of stones, not a finished building. He gave wheat, not bread; he gave the grape, not wine; he gave the nature of wool, not a garment; he gave earth that yields gold, but not gold itself. Why? Because he makes man in the image of God, he shares his work of creation with him: he himself creates, and by man's art he gives shape to what he has created. Because he makes man after his own image, he shares with him the nobility of the things that have come to be. He himself works as Creator, and as God, who brought all things from non-being into being, he himself produces the nature that did not exist; but he allows his image to adorn what has been made. Think who the man was who first put together a plough: how he thought to cut the wood, to fit iron into the middle, to fasten it with joints, to devise a yoke, to set it straight, to bring the oxen together. The wood was there, the iron was there, but the art was not. Who told you, man, that a plough is put together in this way? Who suggested to you that you soften the unyielding nature of iron with fire? Who showed you how to make a tiny needle from so thick a mass? Who conceived in his mind of building doorways out of stones? Where did you learn the idea of roofs? Tell me, man. "You are greatly surprised," he says, "like someone without experience. You see the image of God, and you ask to learn?"

That is why, brothers, human nature everywhere imitates its Master and adorns nature with art. As long as it imitates with moderation, it is good; but when it goes beyond due measure, it is disgraced by its excess. For example, it devised how to subdue the ox, the horse, the camel, and all the irrational animals that were given for its service. But out of greed it devised the mixing of things contrary to nature. It crossed the donkey with the horse, though God did not will it, having said from the beginning, "Let the earth bring forth four-footed animals and creeping things according to their kind." Greed mixed what is contrary to nature, and God, punishing the excess, made the invention barren. That is why the mule does not bear young: it is not one of those creatures made then, which heard, "Increase and fill the earth." Even so, before it acts, he allows the image what it wishes, so as to display its power and to punish its excess.

Again, excessive desire set out to make a human form, imitating, so it says, God at work. It makes the image of a body and forces nature by art. Having heard that God made and shaped man from the earth, art, unable to imitate its Master in truth, contrives the impossible by its inventions. It gathers roots and mixes colours, and imitates an eye that is open, seeing and not seeing; an ear spread open but not hearing; nostrils stretched straight but unable to draw breath; a mouth carefully formed but deprived of voice; feet well proportioned but with no fitness for running. This was to show what he had allowed to the image, as if to say, "So that my own working may be shown." He did not allow it to lay hold of everything, lest it fall into arrogance and despair even of its own salvation. Yet he allowed painters to make things from earth, to put to shame those who deny that God shaped man from the earth. Another art imitated the Creator. It saw a body cut by iron, for instance where some part of the flesh had been cut away by a blade. The hollow must be filled up; the eaten-away flesh must be built up again. It is no creator, able to fashion flesh. What then? The art of the image, imitating the nature of its Master, ran to the earth from which the body comes. It prepares medicines and makes plasters: one cleanses, the other builds up.

And see the wonder. God sits like a father and teacher, watching the works of his own image. A father asks his son, "What does this idea mean?", not in order to learn but in order to test him. In the same way the fountain of good things is always teaching his own image and setting problems before it. He brought the irrational animals and the birds to Adam "to see what he would call them," not so that he who foreknows all things might learn, but to test whether the image was fit for understanding. In came the builder's art, then the carpenter's, the sailor's, the smith's, the tailor's, and the study of the stars: not the meddlesome kind, but the kind that observes their positions, useful to sailors, that watches the risings of the stars and recognizes the season for good sailing. Not the kind that fabricates horoscopes and tells tales of fate, but the kind that follows the Master's voice: "Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them be for signs and for days and for seasons."

The image went forth and explores nature. It seeks herbs and finds them; it seeks roots and lays hold of them. It proves to be the craftsman and inventor of everything. But so that it would not think it had found these things by itself, and not from him who placed the power in its nature, he shows in a single sentence that God is the teacher of our nature in all these things. The blessed Solomon came forward and said: "For he himself gave me unerring knowledge of what exists, to know the structure of the world and the working of the elements, the beginning and end and middle of times, the cycles of the year and the positions of the stars, the natures of living things and the tempers of wild beasts, the varieties of plants and the powers of roots. All things both hidden and manifest I came to know," I, man, the image. How did you know them? "For wisdom, the craftsman of all things, taught me." She taught you what is within measure, not what is beyond it. See into how many excesses human art has poured itself out, even though it was the image of God. It considered how the instrument of the voice produces sound, and studying nature it imitates nature by art. It invents the sound of the organ, the instrument of many pipes, woven together from many reeds. And see what it does, how precisely art has fitted itself to nature. It invented bellows that do not produce air from themselves, but open out and borrow air from outside. Then, from the two bellows into a wind-chest, sending the air into all the pipes, it devised a way for the air to flow and yet produce no sound until the finger shapes the note. Where did this come from, O man? How did you construct an instrument and a container for air? Why does the flowing air make no sound when the pipes are open? "You are greatly surprised," he says, "like someone without experience. I said it before: I am the image of God. I looked at my own nature and imitated myself." How did you imitate yourself? "I saw that in me too this breath is borrowed. For the chest, constantly expanding and contracting, takes in the inflow of breath. I see two airways sending the breath on. It passes to the mouth as through a pipe. I see that the breath goes forward, yet speech does not come about unless the tongue shapes the sound. I looked at myself and copied myself. From myself I grasped the Master's art, as David says: 'Your knowledge has been made wonderful from me.' I looked at myself and praised the craftsman. I imitated my own Master; by art I represented nature."

For the instrument is not bad in itself, but when it becomes an instrument of shameful songs … [?] if they had been called divine from the beginning, they would not have been profane. Even if they were devised in excess for luxury, still, had they been consecrated to God as they were from the beginning, they would not have been profane. That is why David says: "Praise him with psaltery and lyre, with strings and organ, with sweet-sounding cymbals, with cymbals of jubilation, with tambourine and dance." If only the invention had not been turned to licentious luxury or to the worship of idols! If it had rendered to God the fruits of what it invented, the invention of the art would not have been blamed. If it had acknowledged the Master, the lyre would not have been blamed. Would that God were proclaimed through the lyre! This is why, when the blessed David made a lyre and sang no shameful hymns with it but offered sacred words, the lyre became both consecrated to God and a means of putting demons to flight. For when a demon was striking King Saul, beating him and throwing him to the ground, then, it says, whenever the blessed David struck up the lyre, Saul was well and found relief. Do you see that no art at all would have been bad if it had been suited to pleasing God? Instead, everything would have turned out for us as we wished.

But what was my purpose in coming from theology to art and the imitation of the image? It was to turn the Lord's words against the heretics. Which words? "Hypocrites, you know how to interpret the face of the sky and of the earth." You have discovered arts and thought up many inventions, and yet you insult the Master and Craftsman of all? You imitated the Master by your art, and you were promised that you would be like him, "after the image and likeness"; and do you proclaim that I, the Creator, am unlike the one who begot me? I set you free when you were subject to sin; and do you summon me, the Master of all, to be subject? "Yes," he says, "for it is written: 'And the Son himself will be subjected.'" It is indeed said, but in a sense fitting God. For what is said is not our own; it is God's message that is being proclaimed. Then, to follow the wording ... I allow those who have heard to know what is meant. [?] So, to follow the wording: in the creation to come, in the resurrection, he will be subjected then, while you become then equal to the angels? For "in the resurrection of the dead," says the Savior, "they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God." Are you raised up from your own rank, while the Son comes down from lordship into subjection? Have you not heard Paul saying, "For the creation was subjected to vanity, because the creation itself groans together until now"? "The creation": which one? Heaven, earth and everything else. "For the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly." To what vanity? To human vanity. Why does he call man vanity? Because man turned away from the image to become like the irrational beasts. "For vanity of vanities, all is vanity." And David says: "Surely all things are vanity, every man living." It was to this vanity, then, to man in his corruption, that the creation was subjected. How was it subjected? The sun rises on the unworthy, the springs gush for the ungrateful, the earth bears its fruit for the thankless. So the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly. For if it had been up to its own choice, it would not willingly have been subjected to the unworthy; it was "because of him who subjected it." And for what purpose is it subjected? "In hope." What hope? "That the creation itself" (Paul is the one saying this) "will be set free from its bondage to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God." Is the creation set free at that time, while the Son is reduced to slavery?

"Search the Scriptures"; do not slander. "Search"; do not meddle. "Search" in faith, not in contradiction. Where did you learn to say, "Was he begotten when he was, or when he was not?" Where did you learn to say, "To beget and to create are the same thing with God"? Did Peter teach you this? Did Paul suggest it? Did the Savior hand these things down to you? Read the Scripture and respect the law. Yet he does not even stand by what he himself says. For when he asks, "Was he begotten when he was, or when he was not?" he is lying, since he is examining something he does not confess. First confess that he was begotten, and then ask whether it was when he was or when he was not. You deny the fact, and then you torture the word? If you do not grant that he was begotten, why do you inquire into his begetting? "Was he begotten when he was, or when he was not?" Grant that he was begotten. First establish that he was begotten, and then inquire. You deny the nature and examine the wording? Are creating and begetting the same thing? Where does the Son come from? Let one of them tell me. Unless the order of the two is clear first, and the meaning then agrees, I cannot say, "To see and to look are the same," for I have said only one thing. But if I say, "To hear and to see are the same," then I seem to be saying that things which differ, not in sight [?] but agreeing in hearing [?], are the same with God. How do you know that creating and begetting are the same? If he both begot and created, you are right to say they are the same. But if, as you claim, he never begot but only created, how can begetting and creating be the same? This is vainglory in words, words empty of the truth of things.

Why do they spin sophistries about begetting and creating? "God," he says, "is simple, and not as we are. We beget with one part and create with another; for instance, we beget with the organs of generation but create with the hand. God is not like that," he says, "for he is simple and without form. In whatever way he begets, in that same way he also creates." Since you make pronouncements about invisible things, puffed up by this ill-timed and empty philosophy, let one of the visible things convince you that things done in the same way do not [?] have the same meaning. Take this hand of mine, which can be seen, so that the refutation of what is invisible may proceed from what is visible. This hand is one in itself, yet it does different things, and what it accomplishes cannot be brought under a single view. For example, with the same hand I create and I overturn. Then, since creating and overturning are done by the same hand, are they the same? No, they are not the same. Since they say, "We beget in one way and create in another," I say in turn: I create in the same way, with the same hand, that I also tear down. With the same hand I both strike and heal. Will striking and healing then be the same? With the same hand I both push down the one who stands and raise up the one who has fallen. With the same hand I both cast a vote and annul the vote. Will casting a vote and annulling it then be the same? Is this not beyond foolish talk? Are these not fables and absurdities? Does not Paul's soul groan, is not Peter indignant, when such people run riot against the divine teaching? You have renounced what belongs to Christ and learned what belongs to others. Have you not heard the Lord saying, "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words"? Many often confess Christ but are ashamed of his words. The heretic confesses Christ, but when he comes to speak of Father and Son, he is ashamed of the term and says, "Did the one who cannot suffer beget? Then it was by an outflowing! Then it was by making!" Do you see that you are ashamed of the term? What folly! They have become hunters of words, not careful examiners of their meaning. For vanity has corrupted everything.

As I have often said, the origins and sources of the heretics are plain to see. If the Church holds a heretical teaching, name the founder of what we have stated. Who gave birth to this "heresy" of ours, as you call it? The apostles proclaimed it from the beginning. After the apostles, the synod at Nicaea confirmed it. And to show that this was the faith of the whole world: out of so many who gathered, only seven dissented, and they were condemned. The whole world agreed as one, because it came from the apostolic dough.

And see what a wonder this is. By God's design the New imitated the Old. When the kings of the Assyrians came against the land of Palestine, Abraham went out against the foreigners, against five kings. The man of faith went out alone. And how many servants did he lead out against them? Three hundred and eighteen, born in his house. As many as Abraham led out against the foreigners, so many did Christ also lead out against the heresies. As many as Abraham led out against the foreigners, or rather enlisted to fight alongside him, so many did Christ also arm alongside himself against the heresies. There were three hundred and eighteen bishops at Nicaea; and there, three hundred and eighteen servants of Abraham born in his house. Why did it say "born in his house"? Because he also had slaves bought with money; but it showed the true members of the household. And now Christ led out, not just anyone at all, but those born in his house, who proclaim him who is from him who is, the living from the living, light from light.

Why do you say "light" and "light"? What difference is there between life and life? What is the distinction? And here is the wonder: the Father was called light, but the Son with an addition. John the evangelist says of the Father, "God is light," but of the Son, "He was the true light." The Father was called light without qualification, since the audacity of heretics does not readily make war on the Father's divinity, although the outrages they dare against Christ carry the insult up to the Father too. Nevertheless, Scripture establishes what is agreed with a simple statement, but fortifies what is disputed with the truth. The Father is light, without addition, for it is enough for him to be proclaimed in order to be known. The Son is light; but so that no one may say, "That one is spiritual light, but this other is spurious," he is "true light." Again, someone might say: just as the sun is light and the moon is light, but one is a great light and the other a small light, so too the Father is light, but great, and the Son is light, but small. To keep him from saying this, Isaiah anticipates him: "Land of Zebulun, land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light." If God is light, and a great light, God is great. If God is light, as John wrote, "God is light," and if God is the great light, then the Son too is great God. Great is the one who begot and great the one begotten; great the root, great the fruit; great the light, and great too the radiance. I know of no small and great; I know one great God, the Trinity. God is great: "the great, the eternal God," says Isaiah; and Paul says: "awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." "Great is God, great is our Lord," as David says, "and great is his strength." But since strength and power are the same ... [?] for "Christ is the power of God." "Great is our Lord": as if he were saying, Great is the Father, great is his Power. "Great is our Lord, and great is his strength." Great strength, since the Holy Spirit too is great power, as the Savior says to the apostles: "Stay in Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high."

But see what sophistries they devise about the power. "The power," he says, "is something that holds the promise of wealth [?]. For the Spirit is not called God," he says, "but a pledge from God." And hear how he argues: "A pledge is part of a gift, not the whole gift but a part of the whole. For it is written," he says, "by the apostle: 'You were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance.' See," he says, "that he is a gift of God, and not God. So then he is a gift and a pledge, a part of the whole." Well then, if you find God too called a portion and not the whole, and a gift and not the whole, what will you do? For it says, "the pledge of the inheritance." What is the pledge? What is the inheritance? What is "the pledge of the inheritance"? The inheritance is a gift from the one who has given it, not the very one who is inherited. So it says: the Spirit is the pledge of our inheritance. If the Spirit's being called a pledge offends your soul, what do you do when you find God called an inheritance? Pay close attention to how he is called not only the one inherited, but even himself an inheritance. Hear David saying: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance." God is "the portion of my inheritance"; the Spirit is "the pledge of the inheritance." If being called "the portion of the inheritance" makes the Father lesser, then being called "the pledge of the inheritance" also lessens the dignity of the Spirit. Elsewhere David says: "Lord, you are my portion in the land of the living." "My portion": who did the apportioning? For if he is one part, he is not the whole. If you are a hunter of words and not an examiner of meanings, nothing stops you from blaspheming even the Father, whom you think you revere. "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance," and "Lord, you are my portion in the land of the living." Why, then, is the self-existent Power called portion and inheritance? Because we receive God by our own choice. Each of us chooses: one chooses error, another receives God, and the God he has chosen becomes the believer's portion. Here is an example of what I mean. It is written to the Levites: "You shall have no portion in the land, for the Lord is their portion." If God's being called a portion does not offend you, why does the Holy Spirit's being called a pledge offend you?

Let us strip away all the confusion of unbelief and receive the faith that is free of confusion. How long, heretic, will you harden your heart like Pharaoh? How long will you refuse to weigh the divine words in the balance? You have reason within you as a balance: weigh the Savior's words. Consider which words concern the flesh and which concern the divinity. Consider what concerns his dignity and what concerns the dispensation, so that what the prophet says about Canaan may not be said of you as well: "Canaan: in his hand is a balance of injustice; he loved to oppress." And David says: "But the sons of men," that is, the heretics, "are vain in the balance, to do injustice." Do you hold a balance and corrupt justice? Look at the Savior's balance: "I and the Father are one." Where is the inequality? Look at the scales of God the Word: "He who has seen me has seen the Father." Where is the pan that sinks, where the one that rises? See the Father setting free and the Son setting free, as he himself says, "Unless the Son sets you free, you are slaves," and as Paul says, "The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free." If the Father sets free, if the Son sets free, if the Spirit sets free, where is the slave? But may all of us escape the yoke of sin and the yoke of heresy and hold to the faith unswervingly.

And let the heretics not be ignorant of what is said. For I have heard many people asking, "Why does he not speak to us about morals? Why not about conduct and decency?" They do not say this out of longing for it, but to escape being refuted. Do you want true correction? You have often heard the great teaching. You have heard about morals: correct your morals. You have heard about conduct: set your conduct in order. But it is just as the Lord said: "John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, 'He has a demon'; the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, 'A glutton and a drunkard.'" Nothing pleases wickedness. If you speak about morals, it says, "I am asking about the faith." If you speak about the faith, it says, "I wanted to hear about conduct." That is why the Savior, rebuking the childishness of wickedness, said: "We played the pipe for you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not beat your breasts." We piped for you with a holy word, with a word full of light, about the right ordering of morals, and you did not listen. We mourned with a word full of toil and grief, lamenting your unbelief, and you did not listen. Neither did you dance when you heard what concerned you, nor did you grieve when you heard what was said against the heresies.

The Baptist came, and they say, "He has a demon." And the Baptist is not indignant, but keeps to his work. Do you see that he suffers the same things as the Savior? The Jews said of the Savior, "He has a demon and is mad. Why do you listen to him?" Is not a Christian blessed who falls under the same insult as his Master? Paul preaches the truth, and Festus says to him, "You are mad, Paul; your great learning is driving you mad." For sober things look like madness to those who are not in their right mind. But he says, "I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking words of soberness and justice." You see the God-inspired boldness that was taken for madness, yet shone brighter than sobriety. John the Baptist hears, "You have a demon," just as the prophets of old heard that they were possessed.

Once the prophet Elisha sent one of his own disciples, a prophet, and said to him: "Go, and you will find Jehu the commander. Take him aside and say to him, 'Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I have anointed you king.' And pour the horn of oil on him and anoint him king." The prophet sends a disciple who is a prophet. He takes the commander, for Jehu was not king at that time, but a commander under the reigning king. He says to him, "Come aside." And taking him aside, he speaks the words and anoints him from the horn. And when he had anointed him, he fled; he went away. Jehu's companions say to him, "Why did this madman come to you?" that is, "Why did this demoniac come?" "Why did this madman come to you?" So from the beginning the prophets were insulted, and so were the apostles. "Why did this madman come to you?" Jehu, afraid that he might spread abroad the word of kingship and put himself in danger (for while a king is reigning, it is dangerous for the rule to pass to another), says, "You know his babbling and his nonsense." He agreed with them, not in his mind but with his voice: "You know his babbling." Then, realizing that the truth is never a laughing matter, the very men who had mocked are eager to learn the truth: "It is not right, Jehu, if you do not tell us. You are wronging your friends; you do wrong to hide the secret." If he is a madman, why do you want to hear the madman's words? "You do wrong, Jehu, if you do not tell us." Wickedness despises what belongs to virtue, yet is in anguish over it. They condemned him as possessed, and at the same time scrutinized his words as true. "Tell us what he told you." "He took me aside." See the strength of the truth: how the glory that was laughed at came to be revered, how the madman of a prophet proved stronger even than laws. He says, "He took me aside and poured the horn of oil on me." And the commanders raised their voices, saying, "Long live the king!" Do you see how at one and the same moment they laughed at the prophecy and marveled at it, condemned it and believed it? You called him possessed, and do you call the man he appointed king?

So neither we, nor our fathers, nor those who come after us should be surprised if we hear from a heretical tongue anything meant to insult us. May it be ours to be insulted for Christ, so that we may be glorified in Christ, both now and in the rest that awaits us there; to whom...
